title: GNN message passing and invariance
summary: Explain how graph neural networks update node representations while respecting neighborhood structure and node ordering.
objectives: Identify oversmoothing as a depth risk

sections.title: Reference depth · Message passing
sections.body: A typical layer builds a message from each neighbor, aggregates the messages with sum, mean, or max, and combines the result with the node’s own state. Because the neighborhood is a set, reordering its nodes should not change the output.

math.explanation: The self-state contribution and the aggregated neighbor message are combined before the nonlinearity. Because $N(v)$ is a set, the aggregator must give the same result after any permutation of the neighbor list.

sections.title: Reference depth · Receptive field
sections.body: One layer sees one-hop neighbors. Stacking layers expands the receptive field, but it also mixes information repeatedly and can make embeddings too similar. Check held-out performance and representation separation rather than assuming deeper is better.

sections.title: Scope boundary
sections.body: This is reference-supported graph depth. Use it to understand the GNN idea and its invariance requirement; do not silently treat every architecture detail as current lecture exam scope.

examples.title: Worked example: permutation invariance
steps: A node has neighbor features [1, 3] and [3, 1] under two different input orders.
A sum aggregator returns 4 in both cases; a mean aggregator returns 2 in both cases.
A sequence-sensitive operation could return different values, which would make the result depend on an arbitrary neighbor ordering.
examples.answer: Set aggregation preserves graph semantics because neighbor order has no meaning.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why is permutation invariance necessary but not sufficient for a useful GNN?
criticalQuestions.angle: A valid set function can still discard information or oversmooth nodes.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Invariance prevents arbitrary ordering effects, but the aggregator and update still need enough expressive power, depth, and regularization for the task.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What evidence would show that another message-passing layer is harmful?
criticalQuestions.angle: Measure validation performance and node-embedding separation as depth increases.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A validation drop accompanied by increasingly similar node embeddings is evidence of oversmoothing or over-mixing.
